chapters.title: The Window Is Not the View
chapters.tease: Your job hands you a window and calls it the world. The trouble starts when you forget it is only a window.

chapters.title: What Is Up To You
chapters.tease: Epictetus learned what is up to you as a slave. His conclusion was not despair, and it might rescue your Tuesday.

chapters.title: The OKR You Cannot Move
chapters.tease: Someone above you set a number. Revenue up thirty percent. Here is why you never actually owned it.

chapters.title: Influence Is Not Control
chapters.tease: There is a middle country between what you control and what you cannot. Most of your working life is spent there.

chapters.title: The Reorg Was Never Yours
chapters.tease: The reorg lands on a Tuesday and takes your project. Look closely at what it actually took.

chapters.title: Noise Wearing a Deadline
chapters.tease: Much of what demands your attention is just noise that has learned to wear a deadline as a costume.

chapters.title: The Ticket and the Territory
chapters.tease: The ticket says add a button. The territory says legacy code, a hidden dependency and three stakeholders imagining different buttons.

chapters.title: Estimates Are Opinions in Costume
chapters.tease: Ask an engineer how long something will take and you get an opinion dressed as a measurement.

chapters.title: The Backlog Will Outlive You
chapters.tease: You will not finish the backlog. Let that land, because it is one of the most liberating facts at work.

chapters.title: Command Only Your Own Hands
chapters.tease: The whole first part folds into one sentence you could tattoo inside a laptop lid.

chapters.title: The Sprint That Slipped
chapters.tease: Two weeks promised, three weeks spent. Now it is retro time, and the room is already looking for someone to blame.

chapters.title: Love the Quarter You Got
chapters.tease: You wanted the quarter with the clean launch and the promised headcount. You got the other one. Here is how to love it.

chapters.title: The Launch That Flopped
chapters.tease: You shipped it. The graph did not move. Here is how to tell the archer from the wind.

chapters.title: Fortune Ships on Fridays
chapters.tease: Same code, same care, wildly different Fridays. The Stoics had a name for the difference: Fortune's wheel.

chapters.title: The Feature Nobody Used
chapters.tease: A quarter of work, and adoption in the low single digits. Time to zoom out until it is the right size.

chapters.title: Amor Fati, Not Amor Roadmap
chapters.tease: It is easy to love the roadmap. It is clean, ambitious and entirely imaginary. Try loving the path instead.

chapters.title: The Bug Was Always Coming
chapters.tease: The bug was in last month's code all along, waiting for the wrong input. How did this get through? It was always coming.

chapters.title: Say Yes to the Retro
chapters.tease: The retro has a bad reputation, often deserved. Done honestly, it is the most Stoic ritual your office accidentally runs.

chapters.title: The Demo Gods Are Fickle
chapters.tease: It worked every time in rehearsal. Then the client joined the call, and the demo chose that moment to fall over.

chapters.title: Will It, or Bear It
chapters.tease: Epictetus says everything that happens, you either willed or must bear. There is no third box, though we live there.

chapters.title: Rehearse the Outage
chapters.tease: The Stoics ran fire drills in their heads. Modern engineering reinvented it and called it chaos engineering.

chapters.title: The Pre-Mortem Is Free
chapters.tease: A post-mortem is paid for in real damage. A pre-mortem costs an hour and a little imaginative discomfort.

chapters.title: Assume the Deploy Fails
chapters.tease: Optimism is a fine disposition and a terrible deployment strategy.

chapters.title: Worst Case, Rehearsed
chapters.tease: Unnamed fears are always larger than named ones. So name the worst case, out loud, and measure it.

chapters.title: The Pager Will Ring
chapters.tease: You are on call this week. The pager will ring. That is not a risk, it is a certainty to prepare for.

chapters.title: Nothing Should Surprise You
chapters.tease: Marcus started his mornings by listing the difficult people he would meet. Three minutes that bought him a whole day.

chapters.title: The Rollback You Wrote First
chapters.tease: Good engineers write the rollback before the release. It turns out the same rule applies to nearly every hard moment.

chapters.title: Fear Is Just Bad Forecasting
chapters.tease: Strip fear down and much of it is a forecast, delivered as dread instead of a probability, and badly calibrated.

chapters.title: The Demo That Cannot Break
chapters.tease: You can build a demo that cannot break. Not by perfecting the software, but by removing every live dependency on luck.

chapters.title: Expect the Expected
chapters.tease: Here is the quiet joke at the end of premeditation: most of what goes wrong was entirely expected.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: The View From Above the Org
chapters.tease: Marcus Aurelius had a favourite trick: rise until the earth is a marble. Try it on your org chart.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: Titles Are Borrowed, Not Owned
chapters.tease: Your title is not yours. It is a costume the company lends you, and it can take it back.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: The Promo You Did Not Get
chapters.tease: The cycle closed and your name was not on the list. Here is what the committee could not touch.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: Politics Is Other People's Weather
chapters.tease: Office politics feels like something done to you. Mostly it is weather, made by other people's ambitions and fears.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: The Skip-Level Sees Less
chapters.tease: We imagine the people above us see more. Often they see less, through a single red or green cell.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: Your Grade Is Not Your Worth
chapters.tease: Somewhere in a system you are L4 or L5. That number sizes your pay. It was never a measure of you.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: The Corner Office Is a Cubicle
chapters.tease: The corner office looks like an arrival. Ask anyone who reached it: it is a cubicle with a better view.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: Reporting Lines Are Drawn in Chalk
chapters.tease: The org chart looks like bedrock. It is drawn in chalk, and the next reorg already has the eraser.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: The Founder Is Also Afraid
chapters.tease: From below, the founder looks like certainty itself. Get closer and you find someone afraid of the runway.

chapters.part: The View From the Org Chart
chapters.title: Zoom Out Until It Shrinks
chapters.tease: The whole part fits in one instruction: when the org chart looms, zoom out until it shrinks to its real size.

chapters.title: Other People's Opinions
chapters.tease: What your colleague thinks of you is a house built on someone else's land. Stop living there.

chapters.title: The Reply-All Storm
chapters.tease: One ill-judged email, forty replies, half the org copied in. The reply-all storm wants your voice. Decline.

chapters.title: The Credit Taker
chapters.tease: Your idea, your late nights, and someone else presented it and collected the nods. Here is what they cannot take.

chapters.title: The Colleague Who Ghosts the PR
chapters.tease: Your pull request has sat unreviewed for four days. Before you read the silence as disrespect, check the reading.

chapters.title: You Cannot Fix Their Judgement
chapters.tease: You explain, they nod, and next week they make the same bad call. You cannot fix another person's judgement.

chapters.title: The Meeting That Should Have Been
chapters.tease: This meeting could have been an email, and everyone in it knows. Here is how not to waste it twice.

chapters.title: Assume the Charitable Read
chapters.tease: The terse message, the colleague who walked past without a hello. Each one can be read as a slight or as nothing.

chapters.title: The Loud One Is Not the Right One
chapters.tease: In every room someone speaks loudest and most confidently, and we mistake the volume for being right.

chapters.title: Disagree, Then Commit
chapters.tease: You argued against it, argued well, and lost. Now you have to build the thing you think is wrong.

chapters.title: Their Anger Is Their Property
chapters.tease: A colleague is angry at you, perhaps in public, perhaps unfairly. You do not have to catch it.

chapters.title: The Inbox Is a Trap
chapters.tease: The inbox looks like a to-do list. It is a to-do list written entirely by other people.

chapters.title: Attention Is the Only Asset
chapters.tease: You will lose the title, the team and eventually the job. Your attention is the one asset you truly own.

chapters.title: Deep Work as Discipline
chapters.tease: The uninterrupted hour on a hard problem is where real work happens. It is also now the rarest state at work.

chapters.title: The Notification Is Not the Task
chapters.tease: A notification arrives and your body treats it as urgent. It is almost never the task.

chapters.title: Presence Beats Presence-Online
chapters.tease: The green dot says you are available. It says nothing about whether you are actually doing anything worthwhile.

chapters.title: The Meeting You Attended Twice
chapters.tease: You were in the meeting, and you were not. Which means you will end up attending it twice.

chapters.title: Context Switching Is a Tax
chapters.tease: Every switch between tasks feels almost free. Across a day, the tax is enormous, and it is paid in attention.

chapters.title: Do the Next Right Thing
chapters.tease: Overwhelm is often not too much work. It is too much looking at too much work, all at once.

chapters.title: The Calendar Is a Confession
chapters.tease: Show me your calendar and I will show you what you actually value, whatever you say you value.

chapters.title: Guard the Gate of Your Focus
chapters.tease: Your mind has a gate, and most people leave it wide open. Then they wonder why their days are fragmented.

chapters.title: The Badge of Busyness
chapters.tease: Ask someone how they are and they say busy, so busy, with a strange note of pride. Seneca would find that sad.

chapters.title: Rest Is Not a Reward
chapters.tease: We treat rest as a prize for being productive enough. That gets the causation exactly backwards.

chapters.title: The Body Keeps the Sprint
chapters.tease: You can override the body's signals for a while, through crunch after crunch. But the body keeps the account.

chapters.title: Overwork Is a Vanity
chapters.tease: There is a hidden vanity in the sixteen hour day: the flattering story that the work cannot go on without you.

chapters.title: Seneca on the Long Hours
chapters.tease: Seneca wrote a memo about long hours two thousand years ago. It still reads like it landed yesterday.

chapters.title: The Weekend You Sold Cheap
chapters.tease: You worked through Saturday and gave up Sunday. Was the weekend worth what you sold it for?

chapters.title: Tired Is Not Committed
chapters.tease: Somewhere along the way, exhaustion got mistaken for dedication. Tired is not committed. Tired is just tired.

chapters.title: The Sabbatical of the Mind
chapters.tease: The answer to the hard problem often arrives in the shower, not at the desk. That is not a coincidence.

chapters.title: Enough Is a Full Day's Work
chapters.tease: At the end of every day one question hangs there: was that enough? For the overworker, the answer is always no.

chapters.title: Recover Before You Break
chapters.tease: The whole part reduces to one practical rule: recover before you break, not after.

chapters.title: The Layoff Email
chapters.tease: It arrives as an email, or an invite with an ominous lack of agenda. The layoff is real. So is what it cannot take.

chapters.title: Identity Is Not Employment
chapters.tease: What do you do? We answer with our job, so losing it can feel like losing ourselves. It was never you.

chapters.title: Severance Is Fortune's Wheel
chapters.tease: The same person, doing the same quality of work, is hired in a boom and laid off in a bust. Meet Fortune's wheel.

chapters.title: The Team That Dissolved
chapters.tease: Sometimes what ends is not your job but your team. That grief is real, and often underestimated.

chapters.title: You Were Always on Loan
chapters.tease: Epictetus said never say you have lost anything, only that you have returned it. That includes your job.

chapters.title: The Exit Interview
chapters.tease: On the way out they ask for an exit interview. It is a small test of character, with temptations both ways.

chapters.title: Grief Is Allowed, Then Work
chapters.tease: Stoicism is not the stiff upper lip. Grief is allowed. It just is not allowed to move in permanently.

chapters.title: The Startup That Folded
chapters.tease: You poured years into the startup, and it folded. Here is the honest accounting of what you actually lost.

chapters.title: Nothing Was Ever Permanent
chapters.tease: Beneath every ending in this part runs one truth the Stoics kept returning to: nothing was ever permanent.

chapters.title: Leave as You Arrived
chapters.tease: Whatever the circumstances of the exit, one thing is fully in your hands: how you leave.

chapters.title: The Number That Is Never Enough
chapters.tease: There is a number in your head at which you will finally feel secure. The cruel joke is that it moves.

chapters.title: Equity Is a Lottery Ticket
chapters.tease: The equity grant comes with a story about the exit. For most holders, it is a lottery ticket dressed as a plan.

chapters.title: Seneca Was Rich and Knew It
chapters.tease: Easy to dismiss Stoic advice on money as the poor making a virtue of necessity. Except Seneca was among the richest men in Rome.

chapters.title: FOMO Is a Tax on Comparison
chapters.tease: The colleague who joined the company that floated. The friend now earning double. FOMO is a tax, and comparison is what it taxes.

chapters.title: The Raise That Didn't Land
chapters.tease: You made the case, you expected it, and the raise did not come. Money makes the verdict feel unarguable. It is not.

chapters.title: Status Is a Rented Room
chapters.tease: Status feels like something you own. It is closer to a rented room, and the landlord is everyone else's opinion.

chapters.title: Enough Is a Decision
chapters.tease: The central move of this part fits in one line: enough is not a quantity you reach. It is a decision you make.

chapters.title: The Colleague Who Cashed Out
chapters.tease: Someone you worked beside cashed out and walked away. You are still at your desk. Here is the Stoic answer.

chapters.title: Wealth Is Not the Same as Free
chapters.tease: The money chase promises freedom. But plenty of wealthy people are profoundly unfree, cuffed by the very gold.

chapters.title: Want What You Already Have
chapters.tease: The most reliable Stoic teaching about desire: stop chasing what you want, and learn to want what you already have.

chapters.title: Marcus Published Nothing
chapters.tease: The most widely read work of Stoic philosophy was never meant to be read. Marcus published nothing.

chapters.title: The Changelog as Journal
chapters.tease: Every serious project keeps a changelog. Held rightly, it is Seneca's evening review written in commits.

chapters.title: Ship, Then Sleep
chapters.tease: Two words that sound trivial and are anything but: ship, then sleep.

chapters.title: The Work Is the Reward
chapters.tease: We treat work as a means to money and status. The deepest Stoic teaching flips it: the work done well is the reward.

chapters.title: Done Is a Direction
chapters.tease: Perfectionism is the enemy of shipping, and shipping is the whole job. Done is a direction, not a destination.

chapters.title: The Craft Outlasts the Company
chapters.tease: Companies are temporary. The craft you build in them is portable, and it is yours.

chapters.title: You Are What You Ship Daily
chapters.tease: It is tempting to measure yourself by the big launch. The truer measure is what you ship on an ordinary Tuesday.

chapters.title: The Small Commit Compounds
chapters.tease: A single small commit changes almost nothing. A thousand of them transform the system.

chapters.title: Leave the Codebase Better
chapters.tease: Leave the codebase better than you found it. An old engineering maxim, and unmistakably a piece of Stoic ethics.

chapters.title: Do the Work, Stay Unbothered
chapters.tease: At the hundredth chapter the whole book reduces to its title: do the work, and stay unbothered.
